summary: This is an April Fools' Day RFC. It proposes two joke ways of encoding Unicode characters, UTF-9 and UTF-18, aimed at systems with 9-bit bytes or 36-bit words, which are not much used today. It humorously contrasts with the real UTF-8.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st joke proposes Unicode formats for computers that store data in 9-bit units. It treats these unusual machines as a reason to redesign character encoding.

subtitle: An April 1st joke proposing Unicode formats for systems that use 9-bit nonets.

tldr.problem: This April 1st RFC jokes that UTF-7, UTF-8, and UTF-16 are inefficient on machines that use 9-bit nonets.
tldr.mechanism: It describes UTF-9, which uses nonets with a continuation bit, and UTF-18, which stores a code point in a pair of nonets.
tldr.outcome: The document is a humorous encoding proposal and does not define an Internet Standard.

today: RFC 4042 is an Informational April 1st joke about UTF-9 and UTF-18. The memo presents sample code but does not specify an Internet Standard.

sections.title: The Nonet Motivation
sections.content:
The RFC says some platforms use 9-bit nonets rather than 8-bit octets and argues that existing Unicode formats can waste bits on those systems. It points to platforms such as the 36-bit PDP-10.

It proposes UTF-9 and UTF-18 as formats designed around nonet storage. The serious technical presentation of this premise, dated 1 April 2005, is the joke.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC imagines that nonet-based computers need their own Unicode formats. The premise is presented with technical detail as an April 1st joke.

sections.title: UTF-9 and UTF-18
sections.content:
UTF-9 stores the low eight bits of a code point in each nonet and uses the high bit to indicate continuation. The RFC says it does not use surrogates and includes examples and conversion routines.

UTF-18 uses a pair of 9-bit nonets to form an 18-bit value. The document describes which Unicode planes it represents and provides sample code in PDP-10 assembly and C.
sections.plainLanguage: UTF-9 uses a high bit to show whether another nonet follows. UTF-18 joins two nonets into one value.

sections.title: Examples, Validation, and Security
sections.content:
The RFC provides routines for converting between Unicode code points and UTF-9 and gives example encodings. It says sample routines omit validity checks and that applications should reject invalid sequences and code points.

Its security section warns that invalid values and overflow can create invalid data or covert channels. It also asks IANA to reserve the charset names UTF-9 and UTF-18.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how the proposed formats could be converted. The RFC says applications should check input rather than trusting the sample routines to validate it.
